```{r load}
# data from data-raw/vignette_method.R
vd <- function(f) system.file("vignette-data", f, package = "knowledge", mustWork = TRUE)
x <- readRDS(vd("method.rds"))
pipe <- x$pipeline
reg <- x$settings
fun <- x$funnel
fsp <- x$funnel_species
ex <- x$examples
pk <- x$picks
gs <- x$gradient_sensitivity
sg <- x$segment_at_site
n0 <- function(v) format(round(v), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
about <- function(v) format(signif(v, 2), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
pc <- function(v, d = 0) paste0(round(100 * v, d), " %")
fn <- function(stage) fun$n[fun$stage == stage]
val <- function(key) gsub(";", ", ", reg$value[reg$key == key], fixed = TRUE)
issue <- function(n) {
  ifelse(is.na(n) | !nzchar(n), "",
         sprintf("[#%s](https://github.com/NewGraphEnvironment/knowledge/issues/%s)", n, n))
}
species <- c(BT = "bull trout", CH = "chinook", CO = "coho", GR = "grayling", RB = "rainbow trout", ST = "steelhead")
key_words <- function(k) {
  sp <- species[[sub("_.*$", "", k)]]
  paste(sp, if (grepl("_rear$", k)) "rearing" else "spawning")
}
# a rule string (size|gradient|near-river) in words
rule_words <- function(r) {
  p <- strsplit(r, "|", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
  size <- if (grepl("^mad>=", p[1])) {
    sprintf("carries at least %s m³/s", sub("^mad>=", "", p[1]))
  } else {
    sprintf("is at least %s m wide", sub("^width>=", "", p[1]))
  }
  slope <- sprintf("no steeper than %s %%", round(100 * as.numeric(sub("^g<=", "", p[2])), 1))
  near <- if (p[3] == "none") "" else {
    q <- sub("^Q([0-9.]+)@D.*$", "\\1", p[3])
    d <- as.numeric(sub("^.*@D", "", p[3]))
    sprintf("; a smaller stream also counts if it passes the slope test and a river carrying at least %s m³/s lies within %s downstream",
            q, if (d >= 1000) paste(d / 1000, "km") else paste(d, "m"))
  }
  paste0(size, ", ", slope, near)
}
# an SVG Graphviz wrote, inline and no wider than the column (printed by a results = "asis" chunk)
svg_inline <- function(s) {
  s <- sub("^[^<]*(<\\?xml[^>]*>)?\\s*(<!DOCTYPE[^>]*>)?\\s*", "", s)
  cat(sub("<svg ", '<svg style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ', s, fixed = TRUE), "\n")
}
esc <- function(v) gsub(">", "&gt;", gsub("<", "&lt;", gsub("&", "&amp;", v, fixed = TRUE), fixed = TRUE), fixed = TRUE)
ch <- pk[pk$key == "CH_rear", ]
eras <- as.numeric(strsplit(reg$value[reg$key == "era_breaks"], ";", fixed = TRUE)[[1]])
st <- x$stability[x$stability$species_code == "CH" & x$stability$stage == "rear", ]
st[] <- lapply(st, function(v) if (all(grepl("^-?[0-9.]+$", v))) as.numeric(v) else v)
# step 8's words: the exact rule returns on most other splits but seldom on a redraw, it always stays a close call, and
# the choosing beats link's rule
stopifnot(nrow(st) == 1, st$seeds_same_rec > st$seeds_n / 2, st$seeds_rec_in_region == st$seeds_n,
          st$boot_rec_share < 0.5, st$honest_dev_rec < st$honest_dev_default,
          # step 2's words: most of the visits dropped at placement are too far from a stream (none within 500 m, or
          # past the snap limits)
          fn("with a usable point") - fn("far_snap") > (fn("FDIS visits") - fn("ws50_mismatch")) / 2)
lost_all <- fn("FDIS visits") - fn("no_link_segment")
lost_place <- fn("FDIS visits") - fn("ws50_mismatch")
stopifnot(fun$n[1] == 51587, nrow(ch) == 1, all(diff(fun$n) <= 0), lost_place / lost_all > 0.5)
# step 3's and the limits' words: on link's minimal network a site with fish starts a segment of its own about as
# often as one without (within a point) and sits on a segment of about the same length (within a tenth); some picks
# are close calls on the Atlas line's slope and some are not. A bundle without the two tables would make every
# comparison logical(0), which stopifnot() passes
stopifnot(!is.null(sg), !is.null(gs), nrow(gs) > 0, abs(sg$at_site_fish - sg$at_site_zero) < 0.01,
          abs(sg$len_fish / sg$len_zero - 1) < 0.1, sum(gs$pick_in_atlas_region) > 0,
          sum(gs$pick_in_atlas_region) < nrow(gs))
# the limits' words name the segments of link's minimal network built on 2026-11-02 (link 0.78.1, link#441), which
# this ledger records; a bundle written on another build must revise them
stopifnot(identical(unname(x$meta$md5[x$meta$ledger]), "c0020082925429d4505315c81234db2c"))
# the limits' words on the slope crews measured (#121): the segment's slope orders sites as the crews' readings do, less
# well than a second reading, and differs from the site by a few points; near every published limit a quarter or more
# of the sites sit on the other side
sgm <- x$site_gradient
sgl <- sgm$limits
# pooled over every limit's band, so a band of a few sites does not set an end of a range
band_n <- sum(sgl$band_visits)
band_flip <- sum(round(sgl$band_flips_pct / 100 * sgl$band_visits)) / band_n
r2 <- function(v) sprintf("%.2f", v)
stopifnot(!is.null(sgm), nrow(sgl) > 0, sgm$segment$spearman > 0.5, sgm$segment$spearman < sgm$yardstick$spearman,
          sgm$segment$absdiff_p50 > 0.01, sgm$segment$absdiff_p50 < 0.05, band_n > 500, band_flip > 0.25,
          band_flip < 0.5)
```

Each species of salmon and trout spawns and rears in some streams and not others, and what is known of its life
history says roughly which: young chinook, for example, rear in larger streams, and in small streams mostly where
those join a river that holds chinook. A fish habitat
definition writes that down as a few limits on a stream's size and slope, so a habitat model can map it. This article
describes how we test those limits against the Province's fish sampling records, where crews electrofished and caught
the species and where they did not. The biology sets the shape of each habitat definition; where the records allow,
they choose its values, and each choice is checked on parts of the province it was not chosen from. A habitat map
steers where conservation and restoration effort goes, and one tuned this way rests on where fish have been found.

The model we tune is [`link`](https://newgraphenvironment.github.io/link/) [@link], an R package that maps where each
species can reach and where it can spawn and rear on BC's streams, running its habitat definitions on the BC Freshwater
Atlas through [`fresh`](https://github.com/NewGraphEnvironment/fresh) [@fresh]. link builds on bcfishpass
[@norris2024smnorrisbcfishpass], which models which streams fish can reach below natural barriers such as falls and
steep slopes, and which could hold spawning or rearing from their slope and size, so that crews can choose where to
look first among more than half a million mapped road and rail crossings and dams. bcfishpass keeps its spawning and
rearing limits in its repository as
[parameter sets](https://github.com/smnorris/bcfishpass/tree/3bd2824c300c5f9c0c041380d412a52987df1ebb/parameters), most
of them an organization's own. A fair guess at where fish spawn and rear is enough to choose which crossings to
look at first; a map that steers conservation and restoration effort is worth testing against where fish were caught.

For every stretch of stream link asks a few plain questions: is it big enough, is it too steep, and can fish get to
it? Each question has a cut-off in a config, so one habitat definition can be run beside another. We try many, keep
the ones that best tell sites with the species from sites without it, and check that they hold where they were not
chosen. The steps below run in order, from the fish records to values link can read.

## What is a threshold, and what does "tuned" mean? {#thresholds}

A **threshold** is one of those cut-offs: a minimum stream size or a maximum slope. A **fish habitat definition** is
the few thresholds a species and life stage uses together, with any exception its biology adds, such as chinook
rearing's allowance for small streams near a large river. A **tuned** threshold is one chosen by the test this article
describes rather than taken from the literature or set by judgment.

For chinook rearing, for example, link's current habitat definition counts a stream as habitat if it
`r rule_words(ch$default)`. The fish records support a habitat definition where it `r rule_words(ch$pick)`. We tested
between `r about(min(pk$rules))` and `r about(max(pk$rules))` candidate habitat definitions for each of the `r nrow(pk)` species and life
stages with enough records. The [chinook rearing article](tuning-chinook-rearing.html) works through one of them in full.

## What happens, in order? {#steps}

The `r nrow(pipe)` steps are each done by one package. Each box links to its package or source; each step links to its section
below.

```{r flow, results = "asis"}
svg_inline(x$svg$flow)
```

```{r step-detail}
# the code and settings of a step, folded under its text
detail <- function(step) {
  p <- pipe[pipe$step == step, ]
  fns <- strsplit(p$functions, ";", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
  code <- vapply(fns, function(f) {
    if (grepl("^fwapg::", f)) {
      sprintf("<a href=\"https://smnorris.github.io/fwapg/03_functions.html#fwa-indexpoint\"><code>%s</code></a>",
              sub("^fwapg::", "", f))
    } else {
      sprintf("<code>%s()</code>", sub("^knowledge::", "", f))
    }
  }, "")
  s <- reg[reg$step == step, ]
  set <- if (nrow(s)) {
    paste0("<li>", esc(s$label), ": ", esc(gsub(";", ", ", s$value)), ifelse(nzchar(s$unit), paste0(" ", s$unit), ""),
           "</li>", collapse = "")
  } else ""
  open <- if (!is.na(p$issue) && nzchar(p$issue)) {
    sprintf("<li>Open work: <a href=\"https://github.com/NewGraphEnvironment/knowledge/issues/%s\">#%s</a></li>",
            p$issue, p$issue)
  } else ""
  paste0("<details><summary>Code and settings</summary><ul>",
         "<li>Run by: ", esc(gsub(";", ", ", p$scripts)), "; ", paste(code, collapse = ", "), "</li>",
         "<li>In: ", esc(p$inputs), ". Out: ", esc(p$outputs), "</li>", set, open, "</ul></details>")
}
```

### 1. `r pipe$label[1]` {#step-1}

The Province's electrofishing records [@provinceofbritishcolumbia2022FisheriesData]: where crews fished, how much
stream they covered, and what they caught. About `r about(fn("FDIS visits"))` site visits. A survey loaded twice is
kept once.

`r detail(1)`

### 2. `r pipe$label[2]` {#step-2}

Each site's map point is moved onto a stream of the BC Freshwater Atlas [@flnrord2021FreshwaterAtlasb], held in a
database by `fwapg` [@norris2024smnorrisfwapg]. Where the record names the site's tributary in a form the Atlas can
check, the site goes to the nearest stream of that tributary, even past a nearer stream, if it lies within
`r val("snap_limit_code")` m, and is dropped if none does. A site with no such record goes to the nearest stream, if
that lies within `r val("snap_limit")` m ([how a site is placed](#snap)). About `r about(fn("FDIS visits") - fn("ws50_mismatch"))` visits are dropped here,
most because the stream is too far away.

`r detail(2)`

### 3. `r pipe$label[3]` {#step-3}

link [@link] cuts the Atlas streams into short segments and records, for each species, whether fish
can reach each one and what link's current habitat definitions call habitat. Its full network also cuts streams where
the species it models have been observed, using `bcfishobs` [@norris2024smnorrisbcfishobs], so a stream-line site that
caught fish is far more likely than one that caught none to start a short segment of its own, and the slope it is
scored on depends on the catch. The habitat definitions here are tuned on link's minimal network, which leaves out
those cuts, and those at crossings and hand-mapped habitat ([why](#cuts)): there a stream-line site that caught fish
starts a segment of its own about as often as one that caught none (`r pc(sg$at_site_fish, 1)` against
`r pc(sg$at_site_zero, 1)`). The observations never score a habitat definition: they say where fish were seen, not where
they were looked for and missed.

`r detail(3)`

### 4. `r pipe$label[4]` {#step-4}

Flows come from `wet` [@wet]. Mostly that is PCIC's modelled streamflow
[@schnorbus2018VICGlacierVICGL; @craig_etal2020Flexiblewatershed], carried onto Atlas streams by New Graph's fork of
`fwapg` [@norris_irvine2026NewGraphEnvironmentfwapg]. Where PCIC's flow does not reach a stream, or carries under a
fifth of wet's estimate on a stream's own line, it is wet's own water balance, fitted to Water Survey of Canada gauges
[@environmentandclimatechangecanada2021NationalWater]. About
`r pc(x$steps[["5"]][["routed"]] / x$steps[["5"]][["kept"]])` of the kept sites use PCIC's flow.

`r detail(4)`

### 5. `r pipe$label[5]` {#step-5}

Each kept site takes its segment's flow, width, access and slope, and the distance downstream to rivers of each size.
The slope is the segment's own, not that of the whole Atlas line the segment was cut from: a line can be gentle at
one end and steep at the other, and averaging it would score a habitat definition on a slope no segment has.
Sites with no usable date, no fished area or time, no known catch, or no segment at their place drop out. About `r about(fn("no_link_segment"))` sites
remain.

`r detail(5)`

### 6. `r pipe$label[6]` {#step-6}

For each species we build thousands of habitat definitions around link's current values: different minimum stream sizes, slope
limits, and an allowance for small streams close to a big river.

`r detail(6)`

### 7. `r pipe$label[7]` {#step-7}

Each habitat definition is scored and chosen as [described below](#se), where a table gives each species' choice. The model also accounts for how much stream was fished, which data set the record comes
from, its period (`r eras[1]` or earlier, `r eras[1] + 1` to `r eras[2]`, or later) and its watershed group, so a habitat definition is not credited for those. A short trial run checks
the scoring before the full run starts.

`r detail(7)`

### 8. `r pipe$label[8]` {#step-8}

Many habitat definitions score almost alike, so the winner could come down to chance. We choose again three ways: with the groups
split `r st$seeds_n` other ways; leaving out one part of the groups, choosing on the rest and scoring the choice on the
part left out, for each part in turn; and on `r val("n_boot")` random redraws of the groups. For chinook rearing the
exact habitat definition came back on `r st$seeds_same_rec` of the `r st$seeds_n` other splits but in only `r pc(st$boot_rec_share)`
of the redraws. It stayed a close call on all `r st$seeds_rec_in_region` splits, and choosing this way scored better than
link's habitat definition on the parts left out (`r n0(st$honest_dev_rec)` against `r n0(st$honest_dev_default)`; lower is
better).

`r detail(8)`

### 9. `r pipe$label[9]` {#step-9}

We fit a smooth curve of how often the species is caught against stream size, distance to the river and slope, and
use it to grade every segment from low to high expected use. A species whose curve predicts no better than no habitat definition at
all gets no grade.

`r detail(9)`

### 10. `r pipe$label[10]` {#step-10}

link's current habitat definition and the chosen one both go through the steps link itself uses, run by `fresh`
[@fresh]: the habitat definition's test, link's hand-entered habitat, and dropping rearing that has no spawning
nearby. On the Bulkley, those last two steps removed `r n0(ex$stages$dropped_default)` of the
`r n0(ex$stages$pre_default)` segments link's habitat definition passed, so we compare whole runs, not the test alone.

`r detail(10)`

### 11. `r pipe$label[11]` {#step-11}

The chosen values are written under link's own parameter names, with the grades, so link can read them.

`r detail(11)`

## How is a site placed? {#snap}

A site's point is matched with every mapped Atlas stream within `r val("snap_search")` m, except the lines that carry
a stream across a watershed group's boundary (edge type `r val("snap_edges_excluded")`). Where the site's record names its
tributary in a form the Atlas can check, the nearest stream of that tributary is taken, kept if it lies within
`r val("snap_limit_code")` m, even when another stream is nearer; with none of its streams that close, the site is
dropped. A site with no such record takes the nearest stream, kept if it lies within `r val("snap_limit")` m.
The table shows three sites: one kept on its nearest stream, one moved past a nearer stream to the tributary its record
names, and one dropped for its distance.

```{r snap}
row_of <- function(e, fate) {
  nb <- e$near
  data.frame(site = e$site$site_visit, fate = fate, stream = nb$blue_line_key,
             name = ifelse(is.na(nb$gnis_name), "(unnamed)", nb$gnis_name), distance_m = nb$distance_m,
             chosen = ifelse(nb$blue_line_key == e$site$blue_line_key, "yes", ""))
}
knitr::kable(rbind(row_of(ex$kept, "kept"), row_of(ex$moved, "moved"), row_of(ex$far, "dropped")),
             col.names = c("site visit", "fate", "Atlas stream", "name", "distance (m)", "snapped to"),
             caption = sprintf("Three %s sites and every Atlas stream within %s m of each.", ex$wsg, val("snap_search")),
             align = "llrlrl", row.names = FALSE)
```

## How are two habitat definitions told apart? {#se}

Each habitat definition gets a **score**: how well "habitat or not" predicts where the species was caught, at sites in watershed
groups that were left out while the model was fitted. Lower is better.

Scores move with the sites we happen to have. The **standard error (SE)** of the difference between two habitat definitions' scores
says how far that difference would move with a different set of watershed groups. Habitat definitions whose scores are within
`r val("se_region")` SE of the best are **close calls**: the records cannot rank them. From the close calls we take
the one that changes link's current habitat definition least.

One SE is a rule of thumb, fixed before the run. It began with pruning classification trees
[@breiman_etal1984ClassificationRegression; as cited in @chen_yang2021OneStandard] and is now a common way to prefer
the simpler of close models [@hastie_etal2009ElementsStatistical]. It is a convention, not a line below which habitat definitions are
equal: there is no evidence it consistently beats taking the best score, though it often picks fewer variables
[@chen_yang2021OneStandard]. The standard error it rests on has no unbiased estimate
[@bengio_grandvalet2004NoUnbiased], and the usual estimate is often too small
[@bengio_grandvalet2004NoUnbiased; @bates_etal2024CrossValidationWhat], though it can also be too large
[@chen_yang2021OneStandard].

`r val("se_strict")` SE is the stricter reading, about the width of a 95 % interval: more habitat definitions become close calls, and
the choice can stay nearer link's habitat definition. Both are reported.

```{r picks}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `species and stage` = vapply(pk$key, key_words, ""),
  `link's habitat definition` = vapply(pk$default, rule_words, ""),
  `close calls at 1 SE` = n0(pk$close_calls),
  `chosen at 1 SE` = vapply(pk$pick, rule_words, ""),
  `close calls at 1.96 SE` = n0(pk$close_calls_strict),
  `chosen at 1.96 SE` = vapply(pk$pick_strict, rule_words, ""),
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "link's current habitat definition and the one chosen at each width of close call, for each species and stage tuned.",
  row.names = FALSE)
```

## Where are fish sampling records lost? {#lost}

Most of the records lost are lost when sites are put on the map (`r pc(lost_place / lost_all)` of the
`r about(lost_all)` dropped). A site far from any stream, or on the wrong tributary, cannot be trusted to sit on the
stream that was fished.

```{r funnel, fig.height = 3, out.width = "100%", fig.cap = "Site visits each step drops, in the order the steps run."}
f <- fun
f$drop <- c(NA, -diff(f$n))
f <- f[-1, ]
f$label <- factor(f$reason, levels = rev(f$reason))
ggplot(f, aes(x = drop, y = label)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0072B2", width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n0(drop)), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 60, size = 3.2, colour = "#333333") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(v) format(v, big.mark = ","), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(x = "site visits dropped", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

Each species then keeps the sites its habitat definitions can speak to: on a stream line (not in a river polygon, a wetland of
`r val("wetland_ha_min")` ha or more or a lake of `r val("lake_ha_min")` ha or more), of a usual fished area, where
link expects the species, with no code that could hide it and no natural barrier to it downstream. The score uses the
groups where the species was caught at some sites and not others.

```{r funnel-species}
w <- stats::reshape(as.data.frame(fsp[, c("species_code", "stage", "n")]), idvar = "species_code",
                    timevar = "stage", direction = "wide")
names(w) <- sub("^n\\.", "", names(w))
gb <- unique(fsp[, c("species_code", "groups_both")])
w$groups <- gb$groups_both[match(w$species_code, gb$species_code)]
w$species_code <- species[w$species_code]
w[-1] <- lapply(w[-1], n0)
knitr::kable(w[, c("species_code", "kept", "stream_branch", "fished_area", "in_range", "not_blocked", "no_barrier",
                   "scored", "groups")],
             col.names = c("species", "kept", "stream line", "fished area", "where expected", "not hidden",
                           "no barrier", "scored", "groups scored"),
             caption = "Rearing site visits per species after each filter.",
             align = "lrrrrrrrr", row.names = FALSE)
```

## Does where link cuts a stream change the habitat definitions? {#cuts}

```{r cuts}
# from data-raw/vignette_cut_points.R, the bundle of the article this section links
cp <- readRDS(vd("cut_points.rds"))
cp_lim <- function(s) {
  v <- cp$setups$grad_max[cp$setups$setup == s]
  stopifnot(length(v) == 1)
  v
}
cp_moved <- cp$other_keys[cp$other_keys$key != "CH_rear" & cp$other_keys$network_moved != "same", ]
gs_ch <- x$gradient_sensitivity$pick[x$gradient_sensitivity$key == "CH_rear"]
# the words: chinook rearing's slope limit differs between the two networks; the network moved the rules of other
# species and stages too (plural); and the bundle's minimal-network pick is this article's own, so a promotion that
# moves chinook rearing stops the build here until data-raw/vignette_cut_points.R is rerun. The bundle's setup
# "published" is link's full network (#145's run), the one published when the bundle was written
stopifnot(cp_lim("published") > cp_lim("minimal"), nrow(cp_moved) >= 2,
          length(unique(sub("_.*$", "", cp_moved$key))) >= 2,
          length(gs_ch) == 1, identical(gs_ch, cp$setups$pick[cp$setups$setup == "minimal"]))
```

It can, and so the habitat definitions here are tuned on link's minimal network. A habitat definition's slope test
reads each segment's own slope, and link's full network cuts some streams at fish records, so a site that caught fish
often starts a short segment whose slope is worked out from the catch upstream. Tuned on the full network, chinook
rearing's steepest slope is `r paste0(signif(100 * cp_lim("published"), 3), " %")` rather than the minimal network's
`r paste0(signif(100 * cp_lim("minimal"), 3), " %")`, and the network moves the habitat definitions of some other
species and stages too. link draws habitat on its full network, where each segment can read the slope of the minimal
segment it lies in ([link#463](https://github.com/NewGraphEnvironment/link/issues/463)), the slope a habitat definition
here was tuned on. The article [Splitting streams at fish records shifts the steepest slope mapped as habitat](tuning-stream-splits.html)
shows it on our own records; these figures come from that article's data, written on `r cp$meta$written` at commit
`r cp$meta$commit`.

## Limits {#limits}

- A site's tributary code can name several Atlas streams, and the site goes to the nearest of them, which need not be
  the one the crew fished (`r issue("91")`).
- On link's minimal network, `r pc(sg$at_site_fish, 1)` of stream-line sites that caught fish start a segment of their
  own, against `r pc(sg$at_site_zero, 1)` of those that caught none, and the median segment is `r n0(sg$len_fish)` m long
  against `r n0(sg$len_zero)` m, so the stretch a site's slope is worked out over hardly depends on what the crew
  caught (`r issue("120")`). Its segments still end at access gradients, which depend on the species link models.
  Scored on the whole Atlas line's slope instead, the chosen habitat definition is a close call for
  `r sum(gs$pick_in_atlas_region)` of the `r nrow(gs)` species and stages (`r issue("92")`); slopes over a fixed length
  would not depend on where streams are cut (`r issue("70")`). How far the cuts move the habitat definitions is
  [above](#cuts).
- The results are on the segments of link's minimal network, built on 2026-11-02
  ([link#441](https://github.com/NewGraphEnvironment/link/issues/441)), which cuts streams at barriers and access
  gradients but not at fish records, crossings or hand-mapped habitat.
- Crews measured the slope of the channel at `r n0(sgm$measured)` of the `r n0(sgm$placed)` placed sites. On the
  stretches the habitat definitions score, link's segment slope puts those sites in much the same order as the crews' readings (a
  rank correlation of `r r2(sgm$segment$spearman)`, where 1 is the same order and a second reading at the same site
  gives `r r2(sgm$yardstick$spearman)`), but differs from the site's by a median of
  `r round(100 * sgm$segment$absdiff_p50, 1)` percentage points. So a tuned slope limit sorts sites well taken
  together, but reads as a slope on the ground only to within a few points: counting each species' sites within one
  step of its own limit (`r n0(band_n)` in all), `r pc(band_flip)` sit on the other side of it as the crews measured
  it (`r issue("121")`).
- Flows are 30-year averages, so no single dry year is in them.

## Which numbers shape the result, and which have been tested? {#settings}

Every number below shapes a result. Each was checked against the code and the run when this article's data were
written. **Source** says where the value came from: a published source, a convention set here, a value inherited
from link or bcfishpass [@norris2024smnorrisbcfishpass], or a value measured from data. **Tested** says whether the
result has been compared with another value. The untested rows come first: they are the work still to do.

Of the `r nrow(reg)` settings, `r sum(reg$tested == "yes")` have been tested and `r sum(reg$tested == "no" & reg$source == "inherited")`
of the untested ones were inherited.

<details><summary>All `r nrow(reg)` settings</summary>

```{r register}
r <- reg[order(reg$tested != "no", reg$source != "inherited", reg$step), ]
knitr::kable(data.frame(setting = r$label, value = gsub(";", ", ", r$value), unit = r$unit, step = r$step,
                        source = r$source, tested = r$tested, issue = issue(r$issue)),
             caption = "The settings, from inst/method/settings.csv.", align = "llllllr", row.names = FALSE)
```

</details>

## Software and citation {#software}

The steps run on the PostgreSQL tools [`fwapg`](https://smnorris.github.io/fwapg/) and New Graph's
[fork](https://github.com/NewGraphEnvironment/fwapg) of it, and on the R packages
[`link`](https://newgraphenvironment.github.io/link/) (segments, access and habitat),
[`wet`](https://newgraphenvironment.github.io/wet/) (flows), [`fresh`](https://newgraphenvironment.github.io/fresh/)
(the habitat tests) and [`knowledge`](https://newgraphenvironment.github.io/knowledge/) (the evidence and the
tuning). This article's data were written on `r x$meta$written` at commit `r x$meta$commit`. To cite this package:

```{r citation, results = "asis"}
cat(format(utils::citation("knowledge"), style = "text"), sep = "\n\n")
```
